notes.meaning: Solomon calls the leaders of every tribe and family to Jerusalem. They are there to move the ark of the covenant into the new temple. The ark was the sacred chest that held God's covenant, his solemn agreement with Israel. David had earlier brought it to a tent on Mount Zion, and now Solomon brings it up to the temple. Matthew Henry says a temple without the ark was like a house with no one living in it.

The people gather in the seventh month, at the Feast of Tabernacles. At this feast Israel remembered living in tents in the wilderness. It fit the moment well, because God's ark was moving from a tent into a lasting house. The temple had been finished almost a year before. Solomon waited for a time when the whole nation would already be in Jerusalem.

The priests carry the ark, and the Levites (the temple helpers from the tribe of Levi) carry the old Tent of Meeting and its holy objects. Matthew Henry notes that this was the ark's last journey, so the priests carried it themselves. The old tent from Gibeon was brought into the temple. Its holiness, as it were, passed into the new house of God.

As the ark arrives, the king and people offer more sheep and oxen than anyone can count. These offerings honored the ark and showed the nation's joy that it finally had a settled home. Israel was rich and at peace, and the people gave part of that wealth back to God.

The priests set the ark in the Most Holy Place, the innermost room of the temple. It rests under the wings of two huge golden cherubim (angel-like figures) that Solomon had made. Their wings spread over the ark and its carrying poles. Matthew Henry sees in this a picture of God's protection over his worship and his people.

The carrying poles were left in the ark, as God's law required. Their ends could be seen from the room just outside, called the Holy Place. Several commentators think the poles helped guide the high priest to the ark in the dark on the yearly Day of Atonement. That was the one day he went in to sprinkle blood for the people's sins. "To this day" shows the account was first written while the temple still stood.

The ark held only the two stone tablets of the law that Moses received at Mount Horeb (Sinai). Hebrews 9:4 also mentions a jar of manna and Aaron's rod. Matthew Henry and others explain that these were kept beside the ark, not inside it. The Geneva notes suggest instead that enemies may have taken them when they captured the ark.

When the priests come out, a cloud fills the temple. It is the glory of the Lord, the visible sign of God's presence, just as at the tabernacle in Moses' day. It showed that God accepted the temple and had come to live there. The priests could not stay to serve, overcome by the awe of God's holiness.

Solomon calms the frightened priests. He reminds them that God had said he would appear in a thick cloud, so this is a sign of favor, not anger. Then he speaks to God, welcoming him into the house built for him to dwell in forever. Matthew Henry adds that the dark cloud reminds us we see God only dimly now, compared with the light of the gospel and of heaven. The Geneva notes say "forever" depended on Israel staying faithful to God.

Solomon turns from the temple to face the people, who stand respectfully, and he blesses them. Matthew Henry says this blessing calmed their fear after the amazing cloud. Adam Clarke thinks it may have been like the priestly blessing, "The Lord bless you and keep you." Moses and David had blessed the people at similar moments.

Solomon praises God for keeping with his hand what he promised with his mouth to David. Until then God had not chosen a city for his house, but he had chosen David to lead his people. The parallel passage in 2 Chronicles 6 adds that God also chose Jerusalem. Matthew Henry says we enjoy God's mercies most when we see how his deeds match his words.

David longed to build God a house. God told him, "You did well to have this in your heart," but said his son would build it. Matthew Henry draws a comfort from this. God accepts sincere good intentions even when he doesn't let us carry them out. Solomon kindly leaves out the reason David was refused, which was that he had shed much blood in war.

God has kept his word. Solomon sits on David's throne and has built the house for the Lord's name, with a place for the ark. "The covenant" inside the ark means the two stone tablets, the sign of God's agreement with Israel. Matthew Henry says any good we do is really God keeping his promise to us, not us keeping our promises to him.

Solomon stands before the altar of burnt offering in the courtyard, in front of all the people. Chronicles says he stood on a bronze platform, and verse 54 shows he knelt to pray. He spreads his hands toward heaven. This was a common way to pray, showing dependence on God and readiness to receive from him. Notably, the king himself leads this prayer, not the high priest.
